name: IAS–INSA–NASI Summer Research Fellowship (SRFP)
section: Big national programs (apply once, many institutes)
duration: 2 months, typically May–July 2027 (guide can agree to other months)
who: Students at UGC/AICTE/accredited Indian institutions: BSc/BS 2nd yr, BE/BTech/BCA 2nd–3rd yr, BPharm 3rd–4th, MSc/MTech/ME 1st yr, integrated MSc/BS-MS 2nd–4th yr, MBBS 2nd–4th yr, Int. PhD 1st–2nd yr. 65%+ average in core subjects from Class X onward. PhD students not eligible. Max two awards lifetime. Also open to college/university teachers.
stipend: Monthly fellowship (₹12,500/mo for students in recent cycles; confirm in the 2027 PDF) + sleeper/second-class train fare. Host institute usually gives hostel.
what: The single biggest research-internship pipeline in India, run jointly by the three national science academies. You name a specific guide (from the approved list) and write a 150–250 word proposal on what you want to do in their lab; the Academy fetches a recommendation from one of your current teachers. Results and guide concurrence come around March–April 2027. It is the standard way external students get into IISc, TIFR-H, NCBS, JNCASR, PRL and the IISERs.
reality: ~1,500–2,000 selected out of tens of thousands. The proposal must be specific to the guide's work. Generic "I love physics" write-ups are the main reason for rejection. If you are not selected, many host labs still take SRFP-style visitors on their own funds; the guide list is a good cold-email directory.

Students whose professor already works with ISRO move fastest, and the RS/GIS route via IIRS/NRSC is the most research-like for geoscience students. name: Google Summer of Code (GSoC)
duration: 12 weeks standard (late May–late Aug), extendable to ~22 weeks (through early Nov)
who: 18+ at registration; a student, or an open-source beginner if you are not a student. Any nationality, but residents of US-embargoed countries are excluded.
stipend: PPP-adjusted by country of residence. India sits at the floor: $750 / $1,500 / $3,000. Paid 45% after midterm, 55% at end.
what: Google pays you to ship a scoped project (90 / 175 / 350 hours) inside a real open-source org, such as Apache, PSF, GNOME, CERN-HSF, KDE, Wikimedia, Blender, Godot, PyTorch-adjacent orgs and dozens of science and ML orgs. 2026: 15,245 applicants, 23,371 proposals, 1,141 accepted across 184 orgs (~7.5% by applicant).
reality: The proposal is graded against your pre-application contributions to that org. Showing up in March with no merged PRs is a near-certain rejection. Most Indian selections come from people who started in Nov–Jan. Pick 1–2 orgs, not 10. See the [6-month plan](#how-to-actually-get-into-gsoc-the-6-month-plan) below.

name: Outreachy
who: 18+; people subject to systemic bias/underrepresentation in tech in their country (in India this includes women, caste-oppressed groups, LGBTQIA+, disabled applicants, and others; you write an essay). Not past Outreachy or GSoC interns. Cannot hold a full-time job or another internship during the term.
stipend: $7,000, paid in installments
what: Two cohorts a year (May, December). You pass an essay-based initial application, then spend a month making recorded contributions to 1–2 projects (GNOME, Debian, Mozilla, Wikimedia, Fedora, Linux kernel, scientific Python, and many more). Mentors pick interns from those who contributed.
reality: The initial application is the real gate: the essays about the bias you face are read seriously, and generic answers get rejected. University students must have 42 consecutive days free of classes and exams inside the internship dates, judged from the official academic calendar (taking a term off does not count). Most Indian semesters fail that test for the December cohort and pass it for May, so students should aim for May.

what: The main pipeline into AI-safety research: 631 alumni since 2021, 220+ papers, ~75% now working in AI alignment, transparency or security. Applications run in stages and end with mentor interviews and work tests; the Empirical track expects real ML engineering, and prior ML research or strong interpretability/evals projects (e.g., from SPAR or ARENA) are the norm among admits. You must already hold (or get on your own) work authorization in the US, UK or Canada and be there for the programme, because Anthropic does not sponsor fellows' visas. From India, that means it only works if you already study or work in one of those countries (for example on OPT after a US degree, or on a UK Graduate visa)

reality: Selection screens for "proof of exceptional" (publications, olympiad/ICPC ranks, shipped products, prior founding). Expect a short form, a screening call and a partner interview. Dropout rate during FORM is high by design; not everyone leaves with a funded company.
